summary: This standards-track document defines the Service Location Protocol, a scalable framework for discovering and selecting network services. With it, computers need less static configuration for network-based applications, which helps as machines become more portable.

eli5.summary: Instead of memorizing where the printer is, your computer asks the network who offers printing nearby.

questions: how to discover network services automatically
what is a slp directory agent
subtitle: A way for computers to find network services by describing them, instead of knowing host names in advance.

tldr.problem: Finding a network service normally means knowing the name of the host that offers it, which needs static configuration that suits portable computers and busy administrators poorly.
tldr.mechanism: User Agents ask for a service by type and attributes, either by multicast to Service Agents or by unicast to a Directory Agent where Service Agents register their services with a lifetime. Scopes divide large sites into manageable groups.
tldr.outcome: SLP aims at enterprise networks, not the global Internet. It offers authentication of registrations through protected scopes but no confidentiality. Later documents updated this RFC.

today: RFC 2165 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 2608 and RFC 2609. Check those documents for the current protocol rather than relying on this version alone.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
Traditionally users find a service by the name of a network host. The Service Location Protocol (SLP) removes that need: the user names the service and supplies a set of attributes describing it, and the protocol binds that description to the network address of the service.

The RFC states the scope plainly. SLP is a dynamic configuration mechanism for applications in local area networks. It is not a global resolution system for the whole Internet, but is intended for enterprise networks with shared services. Where many clients or services exist, the protocol makes use of nearby Directory Agents that act as a central repository.
sections.eli5: You ask for what you want, such as a printer with color, not for a machine name. The network works out where one is.

sections.title: The Three Kinds of Agent
sections.content:
The protocol has three roles. A User Agent (UA) works for the user to acquire service information. A Service Agent (SA) advertises one or more services. A Directory Agent (DA) collects information from Service Agents into a single repository for efficient access by User Agents. The service itself is reached by some mechanism outside SLP.

A service is described by a Service Type string, which names a template (a "service scheme") of expected attributes, values and protocol behavior. Types are catalogued by a Naming Authority, with IANA as the default. Types beginning with x- are guaranteed not to clash with registered types and are suggested for experimental or private use. A service location is a URL in the service: scheme, and attributes are (class, value-list) pairs. A predicate is a boolean expression over attributes used to select services.
sections.eli5: There are people who look for things, things that can be found, and an optional helper with a big address book. Each kind of thing has a type name, like a label on a drawer.

sections.title: How Discovery Works
sections.content:
A UA that already knows a Directory Agent unicasts its request there and gets a unicast reply. The UA retries until it gets a reply, so a DA with nothing to report must return a response with zero values, possibly with an error code. A UA with no known DA multicasts the request to the service-specific multicast address, and every listening Service Agent that can satisfy it replies. Service Agents with no information MUST NOT respond.

To list ALL matches, the UA resends the request with a list of previous responders, and only agents not on the list answer. Around 60 previous responders fit in one datagram.

Service Agents MUST register with an available DA, and registrations carry a lifetime so that they expire unless refreshed. When a service goes away it should be deregistered, and the DA acknowledges both registration and deregistration. Replies are valid only at delivery, so applications MUST be prepared for stale or incomplete information.

A UA or SA that has no DA can find one by static configuration (discouraged unless multicast and broadcast are impossible), by DHCP (options 78 and 79 are assigned for this), by a Directory Agent Discovery request sent to a multicast address, or passively by hearing unsolicited DA Advertisements.
sections.eli5: You can shout to the whole room and everyone who can help answers. Or you can ask the receptionist, who knows where everything is. Shops tell the receptionist when they open and when they close.

sections.title: Scaling with Directory Agents and Scopes
sections.content:
The RFC describes three operating modes. With no DA, which is meant for a LAN, UAs multicast and SAs reply. With one or more DAs and no scopes, the protocol scales to a group of interconnected LANs with a limited number of hosts. With DAs and scopes, it can be used in an internetworked campus environment.

A scope is a logical grouping of services, typically along administrative lines such as a department or building. DAs advertise their scopes in the attribute class SCOPE. A Service Agent should register with every DA of its scope and with all DAs that have no scope. Scoped DAs do not accept unscoped registrations or requests. The RFC warns that in a large campus having ANY unscoped DA is a bad idea, since it attracts all registrations and becomes a scaling problem. The scope names LOCAL and REMOTE are reserved and SHOULD NOT be used.

Scope membership is open to all unless an external mechanism limits it. A protected scope additionally defines who may register: its DAs reject registrations from agents that cannot give cryptographically strong proof of authorization.
sections.eli5: A big school has a front desk for each building. You ask the desk for your own building. If one desk has no building label, everyone crowds around it, so that is a bad idea.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
All messages share a header with Version (1), Function, Length, a set of flag bits, Dialect, Language Code, Char Encoding and a transaction identifier (XID). The flags are O (overflow), M (monolingual), U (URL authentication present), A (attribute authentication present) and F (new entry in a Service Acknowledgement). Reserved bits and Dialect MUST be zero, and it is an error to set A without U. Only the datagram headers are not human readable; strings are not null-terminated.

There are ten message types: Service Request, Service Reply, Service Registration, Service Deregister, Service Acknowledge, Attribute Request, Attribute Reply, DA Advertisement, Service Type Request and Service Type Reply.

A requester picks the XID from a random seed and increments it per request. A retransmission keeps the same XID so the responder can answer from a brief cache. Since all actions are idempotent, repeating a registration with a new XID extends its lifetime.

Requests have the form <srvtype>[.<na>]/[<scope>]/[<where>]/ and the punctuation is needed even when fields are omitted. A Directory Agent Discovery request is the Service Request directory-agent///, answered with a DA Advertisement.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with the same label saying what kind of message it is, how long it is, and a number so replies can be matched to questions.

sections.title: UDP, TCP and Large Replies
sections.content:
SLP requires both UDP and TCP, with TCP used for bulk transfer only when necessary. Connections are always started by a requesting or registering agent, never by a replying DA. Agents send from ephemeral ports to the Service Location port, 427.

If a reply would not fit in one datagram, the responder returns as much as fits with the Overflow bit set, and the UA reissues the request over TCP. If no MTU information is available, assume an MTU of 1400, which must be configurable. A large registration should likewise be sent over a TCP connection. The initiating agent closes the connection, and DAs and SAs SHOULD eventually close idle ones, with a default of 5 minutes.
sections.eli5: Short answers fit on a postcard. If the answer is too long, the reply says, "Too long, call me instead," and you open a proper phone line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SLP can authenticate Service Agents as part of the scope mechanism, and so protect the integrity of registrations. It does not provide confidentiality; sites that need it should use IP Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 1827).

With unprotected scopes an adversary can easily advertise services on servers it controls, gaining access to users' private information, and can more easily mount selective denial of service. Authentication blocks carry a timestamp and a digital signature. Agents using protected scopes SHOULD implement md5WithRSAEncryption for the signature. Using protected scopes requires cryptographic information to be preconfigured, because without any prior configuration, "blind faith" is required.
sections.eli5: Anyone can put a fake sign on a shop door in an open neighborhood. A protected scope is a neighborhood where each shop has a signature that can be checked, but messages are still not secret.

sections.title: Parameters and Defaults
sections.content:
The RFC fixes a few numbers and leaves others configurable. UDP and TCP port 427 is used for requests to Directory Agents. The Service Location General Multicast Address is 224.0.1.22 and the Directory Agent Discovery Multicast Address is 224.0.1.35. Service-specific multicast addresses come from a range of 1024 contiguous addresses to be assigned by IANA, picked by hashing the Service Type string into the range 0 to 1023.

Defaults include a multicast radius of 32, a path MTU of 1400, a registration lifetime of 10800 seconds (3 hours), and a DA heartbeat every 3 hours. Error codes run from 0 (no error) to 7 (AUTHENTICATION_FAILED).
sections.eli5: Some numbers are like fixed phone numbers everybody must know. Others are timers the school can change.

items.title: No DA
items.text: For a LAN. UAs multicast; SAs reply. No administration needed.

items.title: DAs, no scopes
items.text: Scales to interconnected LANs with a limited number of hosts.

items.title: DAs with scopes
items.text: For an internetworked campus. Needs a coherent plan for assigning scopes.
